(a) Same sequence fragment shown in Figure 4.2, with codons delineated from the first reading frame; the highlighted region indicates an Open Reading Frame (ORF); (b) ORF translation product.

to believe. The first-frame start codon is encountered around a third of the way through the sequence, and the first-frame stop codon appears towards the end, as shown by the highlighted region.

Now we have made progress: we've identified what we believe to be a likely message region, or Open Reading Frame (ORF) – the longest piece of sequence between an frame and an in-frame stop codon. We can now translate this sequence using the genetic code to discover the putative protein (Figure 4.3(b)) – see Box 4.1 for more details.

## Box 4.1 Using the genetic code to translate an ORF

When a reading frame has been correctly established, the codons must be translated into amino acids via the genetic code to reveal the encoded message. This is a simple stepwise process of mapping each codon to its position in the frame and assigning the relevant amino acid. As shown in Figure 4.4, this sequence begins with the start codon, which encodes methionine, and continues with codons for leucine, glutamic acid, leucine, and so on, terminating with the stop codon (which does not encode an amino acid).
